For $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^p}\,dx$, state the condition on $p$ for convergence, and explain why using the antiderivative $\frac{x^{1-p}}{1-p}$ (for $p\neq1$).
questions.answer: Converges when $p>1$. As $b\to\infty$, $b^{1-p}\to0$ only when $1-p<0$, i.e. $p>1$; otherwise the limit is infinite (or, for $p=1$, the antiderivative is $\ln x$, which also diverges).

sections.heading: Improper integrals with infinite discontinuities inside the interval

questions.q: Evaluate $\int_0^2 \frac{1}{(x-1)^2}\,dx$, or explain why it diverges (note the integrand is undefined at $x=1$, inside the interval).
questions.answer: Split at $x=1$: $\int_0^1\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}dx + \int_1^2\frac{1}{(x-1)^2}dx$. Near $x=1$ from either side, $\lim_{b\to1}\left[-\frac{1}{x-1}\right]$ blows up to $\pm\infty$: both pieces diverge, so the full integral diverges.

questions.q: Evaluate $\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{x^{1/3}}\,dx$ (an odd function with a discontinuity at $x=0$), splitting at $x=0$.
questions.answer: By symmetry (odd integrand), $\int_{-1}^0 x^{-1/3}dx = -\int_0^1 x^{-1/3}dx$ (each piece converges since $p=\frac{1}{3}<1$ for this type of integrand near a finite discontinuity). The two pieces cancel: the integral equals $0$.

sections.heading: Visualizing an improper integral as a limiting area

questions.q: The graph shows $f(x)=\frac{1}{x^2}$ on $[1,10]$. As the right boundary extends to infinity, the shaded area approaches a finite limit. Explain why this is plausible, using the fact that $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx=1$ (found earlier).
questions.answer: The curve $y=\frac{1}{x^2}$ decreases rapidly toward $0$, so the strips added as $x$ grows contribute less and less area. Even though the region extends infinitely far right, the total shaded area converges to a finite value, $1$, because the tail contributions shrink fast enough (consistent with the $p$-test, $p=2>1$).

sections.heading: Arc length of a more involved curve

questions.q: Set up (do not evaluate) the arc length integral for $y=x^2$ on $[0,2]$, and estimate it using the straight-line distance between the endpoints as a lower bound.
questions.answer: $y'=2x$: $L=\int_0^2\sqrt{1+4x^2}\,dx$. Straight-line distance between $(0,0)$ and $(2,4)$: $\sqrt{4+16}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5}\approx4.47$, which is a lower bound since the actual curve is longer than the chord connecting its endpoints.

questions.q: Use a comparison with $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$ (known to converge) to argue that $\int_1^\infty \frac{1}{x^2+1}\,dx$ also converges, without evaluating it.
questions.answer: For $x\geq1$, $\frac{1}{x^2+1}<\frac{1}{x^2}$. Since $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$ converges (to $1$), and the integrand of interest is smaller and positive everywhere on $[1,\infty)$, the comparison test guarantees $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x^2+1}\,dx$ also converges.

questions.q: Use a comparison with $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x}\,dx$ (known to diverge) to argue that $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx$ also diverges.
questions.answer: For $x\geq1$, $\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\geq\frac{1}{x}$ (since $\sqrt{x}\leq x$). Since $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x}\,dx$ diverges and the integrand of interest is even larger, the comparison test guarantees $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx$ also diverges.
